section.heading: 3.5 Other Strategies for Integration
Learning Objectives

list.item: Use a table of integrals to solve integration problems.
Use a computer algebra system (CAS) to solve integration problems.

section.paragraph: In addition to the techniques of integration we have already seen, several other tools are widely available to assist with the process of integration. Among these tools are integration tables, which are readily available in many books, including the appendices to this one. Also widely available are computer algebra systems (CAS), which are found on calculators and in many campus computer labs, and are free online.
section.heading: Tables of Integrals
section.paragraph: Integration tables, if used in the right manner, can be a handy way either to evaluate or check an integral quickly. Keep in mind that when using a table to check an answer, it is possible for two completely correct solutions to look very different. For example, in Trigonometric Substitution, we found that, by using the substitution $$x = \tan \theta,$$ we can arrive at
However, using $$x = \sinh \theta,$$ we obtained a different solution—namely,

We later showed algebraically that the two solutions are equivalent. That is, we showed that $$\sinh^{-1}x = \ln \left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right).$$ In this case, the two antiderivatives that we found were actually equal. This need not be the case. However, as long as the difference in the two antiderivatives is a constant, they are equivalent.

example.title: Using a Formula from a Table to Evaluate an Integral

solution.paragraph: If we look at integration tables, we see that several formulas contain expressions of the form $$\sqrt{a^{2} - u^{2}}.$$ This expression is actually similar to $$\sqrt{16 - e^{2x}},$$ where $$a = 4$$ and $$u = e^{x}.$$ Keep in mind that we must also have $$du = e^{x}{dx}.$$ Multiplying the numerator and the denominator of the given integral by $$e^{x}$$ should help to put this integral in a useful form. Thus, we now have
Substituting $$u = e^{x}$$ and $$du = e^{x}{dx}$$ produces $$\int{\frac{\sqrt{a^{2} - u^{2}}}{u^{2}}du.}$$ From the integration table (#88 in Appendix A),

$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\int{\frac{\sqrt{16 - e^{2x}}}{e^{x}}dx}} & {= {\int{\frac{\sqrt{16 - e^{2x}}}{e^{2x}}e^{x}dx}}} & & & { \text{Substitute} u = e^{x} \text{and} du = e^{x}dx.} \\ & {= {\int{\frac{\sqrt{4^{2} - u^{2}}}{u^{2}}du}}} & & & { \text{Apply the formula using} a = 4.} \\ & {= - \frac{\sqrt{4^{2} - u^{2}}}{u} - \sin^{-1}\frac{u}{4} + C} & & & { \text{Substitute} u = e^{x}.} \\ & {= - \frac{\sqrt{16 - e^{2x}}}{e^{x}} - \sin^{-1}\left( \frac{e^{x}}{4} \right) + C.} & & & \end{array}$$

section.heading: Computer Algebra Systems
section.paragraph: If available, a CAS is a faster alternative to a table for solving an integration problem. Many such systems are widely available and are, in general, quite easy to use.

example.title: Using a Computer Algebra System to Evaluate an Integral

problem.paragraph: Use a computer algebra system to evaluate $$\int{\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}.}$$ Compare this result with $$\ln \left| {\frac{\sqrt{x^{2} - 4}}{2} + \frac{x}{2}} \right| + C,$$ a result we might have obtained if we had used trigonometric substitution.

solution.paragraph: Since these two antiderivatives differ by only a constant, the solutions are equivalent. We could have also demonstrated that each of these antiderivatives is correct by differentiating them.

note.title: Media

example.title: Using a CAS to Evaluate an Integral

problem.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int^{}\sin^{3}x dx$$ using a CAS. Compare the result to $$\frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x + C,$$ the result we might have obtained using the technique for integrating odd powers of $$\sin x$$ discussed earlier in this chapter.

solution.paragraph: This looks quite different from $$\frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x + C.$$ To see that these antiderivatives are equivalent, we can make use of a few trigonometric identities:

$$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{1}{12}(\cos \left( {3x} \right) - 9\cos x)} & {= \frac{1}{12}(\cos \left( {x + 2x} \right) - 9\cos x)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{12}(\cos (x)\cos \left( {2x} \right) - \sin (x)\sin \left( {2x} \right) - 9\cos x)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{12}(\cos x\left( {2\cos^{2}x - 1} \right) - \sin x\left( {2\sin x\cos x} \right) - 9\cos x)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{12}(2\cos^{3}x - \cos x - 2\cos x\left( {1 - \cos^{2}x} \right) - 9\cos x)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{12}(4\cos^{3}x - 12\cos x)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x.} \end{array}$$
Thus, the two antiderivatives are identical.
